overlap.title: “Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon … did build” — where had the ark been?
overlap.summary: In Josiah’s eighteenth year the king tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the house Solomon built, and that it shall no longer be a burden on their shoulders. Chronicles had the priests bring the ark into that house at its dedication. The verses checked do not say that the ark had left the house, or where it was when Josiah spoke.
overlap.reasoning: A command to put the ark in the house, with the remark about carrying it on the shoulder, reads as if the ark were not then in its place. Where it had been, and since when, bears on what had happened to the temple’s chief object in the reigns before Josiah. The verses checked report its entry under Solomon and then this command, without describing its intervening movements in those quotations.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the quoted verses state: that the ark had been taken out under an earlier king and kept elsewhere; that it had been moved while the house was repaired; that Levites had been carrying it about; that the words mean “leave the ark in the house” and it had never left. What the verses do state is the command, the house named, and that the ark shall not be a burden on the shoulders. Brenton’s Greek has a statement where the KJV and the Hebrew have a command: “and they put the holy ark in the house”; it likewise does not say where the ark had been. Check made: the four verses quoted were read in the KJV, and 35:3 in the Hebrew and in Brenton’s Greek; a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “ark” finds thirteen verses in 2 Chronicles, none between 8:11 and 35:3, and no verse in 2 Kings. That is a word search, not a reading of those books. These checked verses do not explicitly settle where the ark was before Josiah’s command. The Greek difference is stated as wording; no G is proposed on it in this record. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

english.quote: And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.

And it shall come to pass, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the Lord, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations.
For thus saith the Lord, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
To fulfil the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths: for as long as she lay desolate she kept sabbath, to fulfil threescore and ten years.

studies.title: Can God be seen?
studies.summary: Exodus describes Moses speaking with God “face to face”; John says no one has seen God. The tension depends on whether “face to face” means literal sight.

studies.title: Judas and the field of blood
studies.summary: Matthew and Acts give different accounts of Judas's death and the field purchase.

studies.title: Water or ground: the animals’ origin
studies.summary: Genesis 1 can sound like birds came from water, while Genesis 2 says ground. The apparent conflict depends on how Genesis 1:20 is translated.

studies.title: Plants before people—or after?
studies.summary: Genesis 1 places vegetation before people; Genesis 2 describes no field plants before a cultivator. Whether this conflicts depends on which plants are meant.

studies.title: David’s census: two different totals
studies.summary: The census totals differ: Israel is 800,000 versus 1.1 million; Judah is 500,000 versus 470,000. Different counting rules are proposed but not established here.

studies.title: Herod, Quirinius, and the birth chronology
studies.summary: Matthew places Jesus’s birth under Herod; Luke links it to Quirinius’s census. The historical chronology creates a tension if the same census is intended.
